eva | tathāhi pradhānatvena arthakriyopayogena bhedyatvena dharmāntaraviśeṣyatvena ādigrahaṇasūcitena vā kriyāvattvādinā tāvat dravyabhāvaḥ | tacca etat sakalamābhāsāntararūpamidamitipradhānaparāmṛśyatayā ullasati rājapuruṣa ityādau (page 247) rājādīnāṃ pradhānaparāmṛśyatvābhāve dravyatvotthāpakānāmuktābhāsānāmaparāmarśāt | prakṛte'pi ghaṭo'yamitiparāmarśe ghaṭaśabdasya arthe guṇabhāvagamanāt tadabhedenaiva idaṃparāmarśaḥ, anyathā arthe'nadhyastaḥ svatantra eva sa śabdo vimṛṣṭo bhavet, asmāt agnerḍhak iti nyāyena, natu arthavācakaḥ | tatrāpi anekaśabdatvadarśane jātivyaktidarśane vā svarūpātmakavācyapravaṇasyaiva vācakasya avabhāsaḥ | nanu evaṃ vācakasya parāmṛśyatā asti,- ityetadeva sandehapatitamidaṃśabdena sākṣādaparāmarśāt | śuklaḥ paṭa iti ca śuklaguṇasya pūrvameva prakāśitaparāmṛṣṭasya viśeṣaṇatākāle na punaḥ prakāśaparāmarśau saṃbhavato'nekajñānālambanatāpakṣe | naca kṛtasaṃketaḥ paṭaśabdaḥ kevalapratītyarho bhavati śuklaguṇavat svabhāvata evavā saṃketakālātprabhṛti vā vācyādhyastasyaiva tasya prakāśanāt, ata eva atra na viśeṣaṇaviśeṣyabhāvaḥ, apitu adhyāsa iti vyavahāraḥ tataśca pṛthagidantāparāmṛśyatvābhāve nāmnaḥ pramātṛtattvāt bhedena parāmarśanamiti sandigdhameva,- ityāśaṅkya āha svanāmnā tu iti | iha prakāśitasya parāmarśābhāve prakāśitatvameva durghaṭamiti darśitam | tataśca yathā bāhyasya nīlasya prakāśamānasya nīlamiti vācakaparāmarśastathā vācakasyāpi prakāśasya avaśyabhāvyaṃ vimarśena | naca tatsvarūpavyatirekeṇa tat vijātīyaṃ śabdāntaramasti sāmānyarūpaṃ vā viśeṣarūpaṃ vā yena tat nīlavācakaviśeṣarūpaṃ vimṛṣṭaṃ bhavet | naca anekaśabdatvāśrayeṇa tatsadṛśena śabdāntareṇa tadvimarśo'navasthayā nīlaparāmarśasyaiva abhāvaprasaṅge nīlaprakāśāyogāt | tasmāt svarūpaparāmarśasvabhāva eva arthasya | yato nīlaśabdaḥ parāmarśakastataḥ svaparaparāmarśakatvameva asya svaprakāśatvam | (page 248) parāmarśo hi prakāśasya satyaḥ svabhāva iti niveditam | pradīpasya tu dṛgāvaraṇakāricchāyābhidhānadharmāsahiṣṇutātma bhāsvaratvaṃ svā
**The word is self-luminous, and the order is only in the objects** We have said that the reflexive-awareness is the very nature of the manifestation. Now the vimarśa on the knowledge-power closes by drawing out two consequences — one about words, one about order. First, the word. When we say "this jar," the "this" seems to be a thing that the word "jar" is pasted onto. But Abhinavagupta shows this is a mistake. The "jar"-word, in the determination, does not stand apart as a free thing that the "this" points at; it is superimposed on the meaning, and the "this"-re-recollection is made with the non-difference. If the word were not superimposed, it would be recalled as a free-standing sound — "from this fire, ḍhak" — not as the speaker of a meaning. The conventional word (like the "cloth"-word after the convention) does not shine by a bare experience, as a quality like "white" does; it shines by being superimposed on the meaning. So the relation of word and meaning is not a distinction of two things but a superimposition (adhyāsa). And this brings us to the word's own nature. If the manifested were not re-recollected, its being- manifested itself would be impossible. As the external blue, being manifested, is re-recollected as "blue," so the word — which is itself a manifestation — necessarily has the reflexive-awareness. There is no further word, general or specific, by which it would be recalled as the blue-speaker; and to call it by another similar word would run into the infinite regress, destroying the blue-re-recollection and so the blue-manifestation itself. Hence the own-form-re-recollection is the very nature of the meaning. And because the "blue"-word is the re-collector, its being able to re-collect itself and the other is its self-luminousness (svaprakāśatva). The lamp makes this clear. The lamp shines, revealing the objects and itself — not because it bears the covering shadow, but because its being-shining is its own. The same is true of the word and of the manifestation: by the same act of shining, it reveals the object and reveals itself. The reflexive-awareness-kindling is both the fruit-ground and the seed-ground of the manifestation. The cognition, shining by itself, by that very shining makes the object shine — it is clearly self-and-other-manifesting. So the lamp is self-and-other-light; the word is self-and-other- re-recollection. Second, the order. We see cognition, memory, determination following one another, ordered in time. But this order, kārikā 21 declares, is only by the place-and-time of the *different cognized* objects. The cognition of the blue, then the memory of it, then the determination — these seem to be a sequence. But in themselves, the reflexive-awareness-resting cognitions are one and order-less (akrama). The order belongs to the objects, to the places and times that the cognized things carry; the awareness that knows them all is one, without sequence, resting in itself. Just as the Lord is free of order though he shows order, so the single reflexive-awareness is order-less, appearing ordered only through the objects' place-and-time. With this, the jñānaśakti vimarśa — the reflexive-awareness of the knowledge-power — comes to its close. The word is self-luminous, the manifestation reveals itself and the other, and the order of our cognitions is only in the objects, while the awareness itself is one and order-less. The knowledge-power is, in the end, the single self-luminous reflexive-awareness, free of order, revealing itself and the world. ---

> The claim is that the essence of light is the reflexive awareness, not the bare showing of objects. > The crystal supplies the contrast: a light that merely showed the world without knowing that it showed > it would be no different from crystal — it would reflect, but be inert. What makes the light conscious > is the self-awareness in the very act of manifesting. The passage then identifies this self-knowing > with the supreme speech (parā-vāk) and with the Lord's freedom and lordship. > > The identification with the Word is the extension: the reflexivity is not a bare self-presence but > the supreme speech from which the lower levels of language descend. This is why the word-joined "I" > need not be a construction — language is the form the self-grasp takes, not something that produces > it. The passage establishes the reflexivity claim; the full account of the powers and the Lordship is > developed in the following vimarśas. parā-vāk (supreme speech) · svātantrya/aiśvarya (freedom/lordship).
